job.style: a rule explained with two contrasting examples

response.passage: In the Cartesian coordinate system, every point is represented by an ordered pair (x, y). The first number, x, represents the horizontal distance from the y-axis, while the second number, y, represents the vertical distance from the x-axis. The origin, where both axes intersect, is defined as (0, 0). A point lying exactly on the x-axis has a y-coordinate of 0, such as (5, 0), while a point on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of 0, such as (0, 3). It is vital to remember that the order of coordinates matters; for instance, the point (1, 4) is located one unit right and four units up, whereas (4, 1) is four units right and one unit up. These are distinct positions. Furthermore, the distance between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is calculated using the square root of the sum of the squares of the differences: the square root of [(x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²]. Because we square the differences, the result is always positive, ensuring the distance remains the same regardless of the order of subtraction. For example, the distance between (2, 0) and (5, 0) is 3 units, calculated as the square root of (5 - 2)².
response.summary: The Cartesian plane uses ordered pairs where position and order are critical. Distances are calculated using a specific formula involving squares to ensure positive results. Axes intersections and origins have fixed coordinate values.
